newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine sugar beet output seen at 26 mln tonnes.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine sugar beet output seen at 26 mln tonnes.

text.p: Ukraine is sticking to its sugar beet harvest forecast of 26 million tonnes, despite drought conditions throughout the summer and cold rains in recent weeks, a senior industry researcher said on Monday.
"We will get about 26 million tonnes of sugar beets this year," Leonid Bershtein, a deputy director of Ukraine's Sugar Research Institute, told Reuters.
"The recent rains have meant little for our beets. This year the drought had a greater influence."
Ukraine's 1995 beet harvest was 30 million tonnes.
Bershtein said the 1996 harvest began two weeks later than usual to allow beets to grow larger.
Less than 10 percent of all beets sown had been gathered, he said, with the harvest expected to end in November.
"We hope our autumn will be long and dry," he said. "We've had cases when the frosts came early and we had to leave most of the beets in the ground."
He said the last sugar test in mid-September showed average sugar content 0.7 percent less than at the same stage in 1995, and blamed this year's tough weather conditions.
Yields for the entire crop would probably be less than 20 tonnes per hectare, compared with 21.9 tonnes last year.
Real sugar content at refineries would probably be no more than 12 percent.
"We only have a third of the necessary fertiliser and we have absolutely no herbicides," Bershtein said. "Old equipment means that we lose about 10 percent of the harvest annually."
Government forecasts put refined sugar output this year at 2.8 to 3.0 million tonnes, down from last year's nearly 3.5 million.
Bershtein said Russia's 10 percent tax on Ukrainian sugar shipments to combat what Moscow says is widespread dumping was not likely to damage Ukraine's industry in the long run.
Most of Ukraine's exports of 1.4 million tonnes of refined sugar in the first half of this year, which were sold at below world prices, went to Russia.

"We do have to improve our relations with Russia," Bershtein said, adding that an absence of proper market conditions between the two countries made it difficult to determine competitive prices for sugar.
"But Russia can't live without Ukrainian sugar and would have to buy it elsewhere -- we'll keep working with Russia."
If Russia did not buy Ukrainian sugar, Ukraine would eventually be forced to reduce the area planted to beet.
